overview: “Slavic tribes” and “Slavonic tribes” are broad map labels for many communities speaking related languages, not one kingdom. Their combined coverage runs from 800 to 1000. The earlier outline stretches implausibly far across different populations and is not a reliable ethnic frontier; the later outline is narrower. Local examples below come from western and central Europe and the eastern Alps. They do not represent every community inside either outline.

periods.title: The earlier mapped century
periods.summary: Ninth-century settlements such as Groß Raden combined homes, workshops and places of worship.

periods.title: Local change and surviving texts
periods.summary: Regional communities developed differently; the Freising Manuscripts preserve early Slovenian words from around the end of this period.

items.text: Slavic languages developed through connected dialects whose boundaries were often fluid. Later written languages grew around different political and cultural centres. Shared vocabulary therefore connects people without making their villages, rulers, customs or later national identities interchangeable.

At ninth-century Groß Raden in present-day northeastern Germany, earlier houses had woven walls and measured about 4 by 5 metres. A hearth stood on the sandy floor. The archaeological remains give a sense of compact living spaces where heat, light and everyday activity gathered around the fire.

Later Groß Raden houses were built from stacked logs and could cover up to 45 square metres. They probably had two rooms, and most had a domed oven. This was a local change in household architecture, visible because later floor plans overlap earlier ones.

An oak-plank path ran through Groß Raden towards an island. Houses stood along both sides in a pattern the museum interprets as planned. The wooden route linked domestic space with the wider settlement, a reminder that streets could be built from trees long before they were paved with asphalt.

Excavators at Groß Raden found textile-making equipment and waste left by comb makers, barrel makers, woodturners and smiths. Such leftovers reveal work that finished objects alone might conceal. A scrap beside a workshop can tell us where something was made, rather than simply where it was eventually used.

Wet conditions also preserved a wooden harrow, an oil press and other equipment at Groß Raden. A harrow helped work the soil; the press shows another stage of processing useful plant materials. These discoveries bring farming and food-related work into a story that might otherwise be dominated by walls and weapons.

At ninth- and tenth-century Raddusch in Lower Lusatia, archaeologists uncovered four wells inside the fort. They supplied water for people and animals. A refuge needed more than strong walls: the people sheltering there still had to drink, prepare food and care for livestock.

A study of 91 adults buried near Church VI at ninth- and tenth-century Mikulčice compared tooth and bone chemistry from the same people. The researchers inferred more millet and less animal protein during childhood than adulthood. Childhood meals were reconstructed from adult remains, giving a glimpse of changes within individual lives.

The Mikulčice study also examined cavities and tooth wear. Dietary differences were associated with differences in dental health, and higher-status people had consumed more animal protein from childhood. These are patterns within this cemetery sample, not a claim that all Slavic children ate the same meals or had the same teeth.

A carved oak plank interpreted as a sacred figure ended up in a Raddusch well during the tenth century. It is now a particularly important museum object. The find preserves a physical trace of local religious practice; the circumstances and intentions behind putting it into the well are less certain.

Groß Raden burned around 900 and was quickly rebuilt with larger log houses and a new island sanctuary. The museum considers the fire probably unrelated to an enemy attack. A burned layer records a destructive event, but identifying an enemy requires evidence beyond charcoal.

sections.title: Learning, care and actual written words

items.text: The Freising Manuscripts contain two confession texts and a sermon in early Slovenian. Scholars place their writing probably shortly before 1000 and connect their use with Upper Carinthia. They preserve one regional Slavic language in Latin letters, showing how religious teaching could use a local language alongside Latin.

The first manuscript begins “GLAGOLITE PO NAƷ REDKA ZLOUEZA·”. Translation: “Say after us [these] few words.” This is Igor Grdina’s transcription of folio 78r, retaining the medieval Latin-letter spelling. The instruction invites listeners to repeat the prayer, offering a direct glimpse of teaching through spoken participation.

The second Freising text praises giving meals and clothing to people in need, visiting the sick and offering shelter to strangers. It is a sermon urging good conduct, rather than proof that every community provided these services. Its examples nevertheless show the kinds of everyday care that a preacher wanted listeners to recognise.

ending.text: The year 1000 ends this map interval, not Slavic-speaking society. Communities continued within different states and religious traditions, and their dialects developed into several written languages. Some local languages later disappeared, while others remain spoken today. There was no single collective fall or successor kingdom.
